summary.text: A 26-year-old man with undiagnosed acromegaly presented to the emergency department with three days of progressive left eye vision loss and left retro-orbital pain, plus sudden right-sided weakness, dizziness and vomiting. Examination showed Glasgow Coma Scale 14/15, left eye light perception, third-degree left ptosis, right facial palsy and power of 1/5 in the right limbs with upper-motor-neuron signs.

evidence.quote: A 26-year-old male presented to our emergency department
his Glasgow Coma Scale was 14/15

summary.text: CT showed a sellar mass and left middle cerebral artery hypodensity, and MRI showed a large hemorrhagic sellar and suprasellar mass compressing the left internal carotid artery. Carotid Doppler showed no thrombosis or significant narrowing. Growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor were high and other pituitary hormones normal. Pituitary apoplexy was diagnosed.

evidence.quote: a sellar mass
Pituitary apoplexy was diagnosed

summary.text: He underwent emergency transcranial craniotomy and tumor excision because of hemiparesis and visual deficit, leaving a small tuft of tumor behind. Histopathology confirmed pituitary adenoma with hemorrhagic infarction, and postoperative CT showed an empty pituitary fossa and a left cortical infarct. Diabetes insipidus developed on the third postoperative day, requiring desmopressin nasal spray, and thyroid hormones and steroids were supplemented. Hypothyroidism also developed postoperatively; the diabetes insipidus corrected eventually, but long-term thyroid hormone and steroid therapy was needed.

summary.text: One week after surgery right limb power had improved to 4 + /5. The vision of the left eye did not improve much, with acuity remaining mild perception of light. At the six-month follow-up he had subtle right upper limb weakness with pronator drift and power 5/5 in the right lower limb. He could walk without external support, and left eye acuity was 6/36 on Snellen chart. The authors report that neurological status improved significantly after the surgery.

article_limitations: Discussion sentences about general pituitary apoplexy literature are background and not patient facts.
The hands and feet statement in the examination paragraph is internally inconsistent and recorded as review-only.

Times of the post-operative left eye visual acuity, of walking without support and of the 6/36 acuity, of the thyroid hormone and steroid supplementation and of the correction of diabetes insipidus are not stated in their own sentences and are left null; these are kept as separate untimed events rather than inside the one-week or six-month events.

Imaging, diagnosis and surgery are not ordered against each other: the diagnosis is "based on" the imaging (basis wording) and the stated surgery indications are clinical deficits and technical factors, not an imaging result.
